kurz: What the efficient market hypothesis claims, what it expressly does not claim and why complete market efficiency would cancel out its own precondition.

bloecke.md:
The [[efficient market hypothesis]] is often quoted and frequently misrepresented in the process. It does not say that prices are correct, that investors act rationally or that excesses are impossible. Its claim is narrower and at the same time stricter. According to it, a price already contains the available information, and for that reason no reliable advantage can be gained from that very information.

Eugene Fama put the claim into a systematic form in the *Journal of Finance* in 1970. In 2013, he received the Nobel Prize in economics for it, together with Lars Peter Hansen and Robert Shiller, who disputes the scope of the hypothesis. The joint award reflects the state of the debate well. The core claim is regarded as undisputed, while its limits are still being argued over.

## The three forms of the hypothesis

Fama orders the three forms solely by the set of information that is supposed to have been processed in the price already. The quality of a market is not a criterion for this. The information sets are nested within each other, so that each stronger form includes the weaker ones.

The **weak form** refers solely to price history, that is, to past prices, trading volumes and chart patterns. If it holds, any trading rule that uses only the past price path is worthless.

The **semi-strong form** additionally includes everything that is publicly available, such as annual reports, ad hoc announcements, analyst research, economic data and newspaper articles. If it holds, even technically flawless fundamental analysis is of no use as long as it processes only public figures, because all other market participants have these figures too.

The **strong form** also includes non-public knowledge. It has been refuted empirically and was never intended as a serious description of markets. It serves to mark the upper limit. The strongest argument against it is that legislators around the world prohibit insider trading. Such a ban would be superfluous if inside knowledge brought no advantage anyway.

bloecke.text: A market in which prices always fully reflect available information is called efficient.
bloecke.quelle: Eugene F. Fama, Efficient Capital Markets, Journal of Finance 1970

bloecke.md:
## Prices as a random walk

The empirical finding is older than the theory. In 1900, Louis Bachelier modelled price movements as a random process in his Paris doctoral thesis. In 1953, Maurice Kendall searched British share and commodity price series for cycles, found none and described prices as wandering aimlessly. Paul Samuelson supplied the theoretical justification afterwards, in 1965. If prices are properly anticipated, their changes must look random. Burton Malkiel popularised the idea in 1973, among other things with the image of a blindfolded monkey throwing darts at the stock listings in the newspaper and thereby obtaining a portfolio that does no worse than the experts' selections.

A predictable price movement would be anticipated immediately. If all investors knew that a share would be 10% higher in four weeks, they would buy today, and the rise would already take place today. What remains is only the part of the movement that no one could have recognised beforehand. The [[random walk]] of prices is thus a consequence of this anticipation.

bloecke.titel: Share of positive following years after down and up years
bloecke.unter: MSCI World, net in euros, calendar years 1970 to 2025. With 15 observations, the difference of just under two percentage points lies well within random fluctuation.

serien.name: Share of positive following years in %

bloecke.md:
From 1970 to 2025, the MSCI World (net, in euros) closed with a loss in 15 of 56 calendar years. If the sign of the previous year were a signal, it would have to show up in the following year.

- After the 15 down years, the following year was positive 11 times, which is 73%.
- After the 40 up years, the following year was positive 30 times, which is 75%.
- The base rate across all 55 following years is 41 positive years, or 74.5%.

The picture is similar for the size of the returns. After down years, the following year brought 7.1% on average, after up years 10.8%. The difference of 3.7 percentage points looks clear, but it is based on only 15 observations. With a dispersion of annual returns of around 19 percentage points, the standard error of a mean over 15 years is just under 5 percentage points. The difference therefore cannot be distinguished from chance.

An efficient price is not automatically a correct valuation. The hypothesis only claims that the price has processed the available information. Whether this information was good is a different question. In hindsight, prices have regularly been wrong. That does not refute the hypothesis as long as the error could not be recognised beforehand.

Unpredictable prices nevertheless have an expected value. The random walk has an upward drift, which is the compensation for the risk borne. Only the deviation around this drift is unpredictable; the drift itself is not. The conclusion that shares are a gamble therefore confuses dispersion with expected value.

## Limits of efficiency tests

Every test needs a benchmark for what return would have been appropriate, that is, a pricing model such as the CAPM or a factor model. If the measurement shows an excess return, there are two possible explanations. Either the market was inefficient, or the model measured the risk incorrectly. The data cannot distinguish between the two explanations. In 1991, Fama called this the joint hypothesis problem. As a consequence, the hypothesis cannot be refuted in a strict reading.

This is also why the dispute between Fama and Shiller cannot be settled. In 1981, Shiller showed that share prices fluctuate more than the dividends subsequently paid justify, and saw this as evidence of excess volatility. Fama counters that the discount rate is not constant. If investors' willingness to take risks fluctuates, prices fluctuate even when cash flows are unchanged. Both interpretations are consistent with the same data.

In practice, the hypothesis should therefore be treated as a benchmark rather than as a law of nature. A more useful question than whether the market is efficient is how efficient a particular segment is and what it costs to exploit a deviation.

## The efficiency paradox

The strongest limitation of the hypothesis arises from the theory itself. In 1980, Sanford Grossman and Joseph Stiglitz showed that in a fully informationally efficient market, no one would have a reason to pay for information. Without paid research, however, the information never gets into the price in the first place. Complete efficiency would thus cancel out its own precondition.

The solution is an equilibrium in which a certain degree of imprecision persists permanently. There must always be enough mispricing for research to just about recover its costs. This leads to a testable prediction. The gross advantage of all information seekers together roughly equals what they spend on the search, so that on average nothing remains after fees. Information seekers therefore do have skill, but it costs about as much as it brings in.

bloecke.unter: Every deviation creates the incentive to eliminate it, and every elimination takes away the next information seeker's reason to search, so that the equilibrium keeps re-establishing itself.

bloecke.md: The efficient market hypothesis describes an equilibrium that keeps re-establishing itself. Deviations arise constantly and are constantly eliminated again. What remains is on average roughly as large as the cost of this elimination. For investors, what matters is therefore whether mispricings are larger than the effort needed to find them. The mere existence of mispricings is not enough.

## Legal foundations of market efficiency

Public information does not enter the price quickly and simultaneously for everyone by itself. In Germany and the EU, statutory obligations ensure that it does.

- Article 17 of the Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014, MAR for short) requires issuers to publish inside information without delay. A delay is permitted only under strict conditions and must be notified to BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority).
- Article 7 MAR defines what inside information is. It must be precise, must not be publicly known and must be likely to have a significant effect on the price.
- Article 14 MAR prohibits insider dealing and the unlawful disclosure of inside information. Section 119 WpHG (Securities Trading Act) makes a breach a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment of up to five years, and Section 120 WpHG governs the fines.
- Article 19 MAR requires executives to report their own transactions in securities of their own company no later than three business days after the transaction. The notifications are published.

The strong form is thus empirically false and at the same time undesirable in law. The semi-strong form, by contrast, is the declared aim of regulation. Where supervision is weak, for example with thinly traded small caps, in unregulated segments or in foreign jurisdictions, efficiency is correspondingly lower.

## Practical implications

The hypothesis does not forbid anyone from being active. It only sets the hurdle that an active decision has to clear. In Germany, this hurdle is higher than the order fee alone, because tax law favours holding investments.

Realised capital gains are income from capital assets, for shares under Section 20(2) EStG (Income Tax Act), for fund units under Section 20(1) no. 3 EStG in conjunction with Section 16(1) no. 3 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). They are charged with 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus the solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% (Section 32d(1) EStG), plus church tax where applicable. For equity funds, the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30% under Section 20 InvStG reduces the tax base, so that effectively around 18.46% is payable on the gain. With annual switching, this rate is incurred every year; if the investment is left alone, it is incurred only once at the end. Until then, the tax amount not yet paid remains invested and continues to earn a return.

The following illustrative calculation puts a figure on this effect for €10,000 at a gross return of 7%. Transaction costs and bid-ask spreads are left out, although they would be added in the switching variant. To that extent, the calculation is deliberately favourable to this variant. The advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG and the [[Saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)]] are also left out. Both would reduce the calculated gap. Even when the investment is left alone, the advance lump sum brings part of the tax forward in years with a positive base interest rate (Basiszins), and the switching variant could use an unused allowance every year. The calculated benefit of the tax deferral is therefore more of an upper limit. The gap thus arises solely from the timing of taxation.

bloecke.unter: €10,000 lump-sum investment, 7% gross a year, equity ETF with 30% partial exemption. Both bars show the wealth after tax on a sale at the respective point in time.

serien.name: left alone, tax only on sale

bloecke.md:
With an effective burden of 18.46%, a gross return of 7.00% leaves 5.71% net a year. Over 30 years, this results in €52,868 instead of €63,915. The gap amounts to around €11,000, or 17% of the final wealth.

Calculated the other way round, the variant that switches every year would need 7.82% instead of 7.00% gross to draw level. In this model, it therefore needs a lead of 0.82 percentage points a year just to offset the tax deferral, and that is before order fees and bid-ask spreads. With the advance lump sum and an otherwise unused saver's allowance, this figure would be lower, and for small portfolios it can disappear entirely. Only when an active decision clears the hurdle of taxes and costs does it make sense to talk about skill at all.

Three levers require no information advantage and therefore work regardless of how efficient the market happens to be. They are the ongoing charges of the investment product, the breadth of diversification and the number of taxable realisations. In addition, there is making full use of the saver's allowance of €1,000 per person, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG), through an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) under Section 44a EStG. These points are not investment recommendations. They are the items whose outcome does not depend on what other market participants do.

Paul Samuelson argued, in essence, that markets are much more efficient at the level of individual securities than at the level of the market as a whole. If a share is mispriced relative to a competitor's share, this corrects itself quickly, because the two securities can be traded against each other. Whether the market as a whole is too expensive, on the other hand, can remain an open question for years, because there is no low-risk offsetting position against the market as a whole.

A similar pattern emerges when different markets are compared. The thinner a market, the fewer analysts follow it and the weaker the disclosure requirements, the more likely deviations are. However, that is also where bid-ask spreads are widest and research effort is greatest. This is the efficiency paradox in practice. Mispricings reliably occur where exploiting them is most expensive.

mitnehmen: The efficient market hypothesis states that available information has already been processed in the price, not that prices are correct; mispricings seen in hindsight therefore do not refute it.
The weak, semi-strong and strong forms differ only in the set of information; the strong form is refuted and legally undesirable, and the semi-strong form is the most disputed.
A random walk does not rule out a positive expected return, because only the deviation around the drift is unpredictable.
Because every efficiency test also tests a pricing model, the thesis cannot be refuted as a statement of fact and serves as a benchmark.
Grossman and Stiglitz show why complete efficiency is impossible and why the remaining advantage is roughly as large as the cost of finding it.

begriffe.text: Variant of the efficient market hypothesis according to which all publicly available information has already been processed in the price. This form is the most hotly disputed in the debate.

Variant of the efficient market hypothesis according to which even non-public knowledge is contained in the price. It has been refuted empirically, and bans on insider trading presuppose that it does not hold.
The problem that every test of market efficiency also tests the assumed pricing model. If the test comes out negative, it remains unclear whether the market was inefficient or the model was wrong.

Obligation of listed issuers under Article 17 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation to publish inside information without delay. It is a legal precondition for prices to absorb public information quickly.

Finding described by Robert Shiller in 1981 that share prices fluctuate more than the dividends subsequently paid justify. It is regarded as the most important empirical objection to the semi-strong form.
